doc.title: Paul Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 14, 1999

title: Novachord, doubles and playing with strings
summary: Studio doubles such as Hammond organ, celeste and Novachord; the Novachord's delay let him sit with strings that play behind the beat.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: Yeah. And you run in there and you’ve got everything in the so-called old days back in the late 40s, 50s, 60s, all your doubles in the studios. I mean once in a while you got to play a Hammond organ and celeste, and then I think the first electronic instrument was the Novachord. And that was kind of a dull thing to play also. The only advantage to it was it had a stop on there where you could delay your sound, the sound would come out about an eighth note late, and you could play perfectly with a string section, because string sections follow the conductor and they’re about an eighth note behind the actual downbeat. You know it’s like daah — they play on the upbeat, and it’s hard to do if you’re a timekeeper. So if you can play in time and push that key and the key sounds an eighth later, you’re right with the strings.

It wasn’t particularly much fun to play, that particular instrument, but I mean it did work that way, if they needed it to blend in with the strings. Because the strings, I mean, it’s just a fact of life that they play just that little bit behind because of the conductor.
Yeah, you don’t get Taa, you kind of get a little—

You can get that if you tell them ahead of time, I mean the good string players, like the guys that do the studios and also the symphonies and all that, I mean if you say I want it when my hand hits the belt buckle, I mean I want boom here, rather than, daaa, on the upbeat, well they’ll come through for you, because they’re all good musicians.
